title: Liberation and Feminist Theology
welcome_lead: Move from the favelas of Latin America to the campuses of North America as theologians reimagine Christianity from the underside of history.
meta_desc: A-Level Religious Studies adventure on liberation theology (Gutierrez) and feminist theology (Daly, Ruether), with their methods and critics.
final_note: You have explored two contextual theologies that read the gospel from below.

walkthroughs.body_html: Gustavo Gutierrez's A Theology of Liberation (1971) defines theology as 'critical reflection on praxis in the light of the Word of God'. Drawing on Vatican II and the Medellin (1968) and Puebla (1979) bishops' conferences, he develops the preferential option for the poor. The Vatican's 1984 and 1986 Instructions distinguished acceptable from unacceptable liberation theology, especially regarding Marxist analysis.

Mary Daly's The Church and the Second Sex (1968) began as a reformist work; Beyond God the Father (1973) declared 'if God is male, then the male is God'. She rejected reformist solutions and pursued a 'post-Christian' feminist theology of the Verb, of Be-ing. Daly's later neologisms in Gyn/Ecology (1978) and Pure Lust (1984) sought to reclaim language itself.

Rosemary Radford Ruether's Sexism and God-Talk (1983) remained within Christianity, identifying a 'prophetic principle' that critiques every patriarchal distortion. She proposed the Christa (Christ as woman) as a constructive image. Critics from within liberation theology argued that gender and race must be integrated; womanist theologians like Delores Williams developed this in Sisters in the Wilderness (1993).
